content: The capital of Indonesia is Jakarta, on the north-west coast of Java. Since 2019 the government has been progressively moving parts of the administrative capital to Nusantara (IKN) in East Kalimantan; Jakarta remains the largest city and economic centre.

Indonesia has three time zones: WIB (Western Indonesia Time, UTC+7 — Java, Sumatra, western/central Kalimantan), WITA (Central Indonesia Time, UTC+8 — Bali, Nusa Tenggara, Sulawesi, eastern Kalimantan), and WIT (Eastern Indonesia Time, UTC+9 — Maluku, Papua).

Indonesia's currency is the Rupiah (IDR, symbol Rp). Bank notes come in denominations of 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000, 20,000, 50,000 and 100,000 Rupiah. Cash is still widely used, but QRIS (a national QR-payment system) is accepted at most cafés, warung and stores.

The official language is Bahasa Indonesia. English is common in tourist areas (Bali, Jakarta, Yogyakarta) but limited elsewhere. Learning a handful of phrases (terima kasih = thank you, permisi = excuse me, tolong = please) is warmly received.

Bali is Indonesia's most-visited province. Key areas: Canggu (surf, cafés, digital nomads), Seminyak (beach clubs, upscale dining), Ubud (rice terraces, yoga, art villages), Sanur (calm, family-friendly beach), Uluwatu (dramatic clifftop sunsets and surf breaks), Nusa Dua (resort strip), Nusa Penida and Nusa Lembongan (day-trip islands with clear water and Kelingking Beach). Peak season roughly July–August and Christmas/New Year.

Yogyakarta (Jogja) is Java's cultural heart. Highlights: Borobudur (world's largest Buddhist temple, sunrise visits limited to timed tickets), Prambanan (Hindu temple complex, evening Ramayana ballet in dry season), Kraton (Sultan's Palace), Malioboro Street (shopping + street food), Kotagede (silver workshops), Mount Merapi jeep tours, and cheap batik courses. A 2–3 day stop is typical.

Lombok is Bali's quieter neighbour. Kuta Lombok (surf beaches, not to be confused with Kuta Bali), Selong Belanak (family-friendly beach), Gili Trawangan/Meno/Air (snorkelling islands, easy fast-boat from Bali), Mount Rinjani trek (2–4 day summit hike, permit required), Sasak villages. Less developed than Bali; bring more cash.

Labuan Bajo (west Flores) is the gateway to Komodo National Park. Common tours: 1-day speedboat (Padar Island viewpoint, Pink Beach, Komodo dragons at Rinca or Komodo Island, Manta Point snorkelling) or 2–3 day liveaboard boats. Dry season (May–October) is best; sea can be rough in wet season.

Nasi goreng is Indonesian fried rice — rice stir-fried with kecap manis (sweet soy sauce), garlic, shallots, chilli and often chicken, egg or prawn. Usually served with a fried egg on top, prawn crackers and slices of cucumber and tomato. Considered the national dish and available almost everywhere from street stalls to hotels.

Rendang is a slow-cooked beef curry from West Sumatra (Padang cuisine). Beef is simmered for hours in coconut milk with lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, kaffir lime and chilli until the liquid reduces and the meat turns dark and rich. Best found at Padang restaurants (rumah makan Padang) — the classic ordering style is a bench of small dishes brought to your table, you pay for what you eat.

Sate (satay) is skewered grilled meat served with a dipping sauce. Common types: sate ayam (chicken, sweet peanut sauce), sate kambing (goat), sate lilit (Balinese minced fish/meat wrapped on lemongrass stems). Look for sate stalls with lit charcoal in the evening — that's when they're at their best.

Indonesia is the world's most-populous Muslim country and most restaurants are halal by default. Notable exceptions: Bali (large Hindu population, pork and alcohol are widely served), Chinese-Indonesian restaurants, and some Balinese specialities like babi guling (roast pork) and babi kecap. If halal matters to you, look for a green halal logo or ask 'halal?'.

Ride-hailing (Gojek, Grab) is standard in cities — cheap, in-app payment, motorbike (ojek) or car options. Away from Bali/Java the coverage thins out; expect to use hotel-arranged drivers or negotiate a day-rate car with driver (~600k–1M IDR per day depending on region). Traffic in Bali (esp. Canggu, Seminyak) is heavy; a motorbike is faster but requires an international driving permit and confidence in local road behaviour.

Cash is still important for small warungs, markets, tips, and rural areas. Withdraw from bank-branch ATMs (BCA, Mandiri, BNI) to avoid the worst skimming risk. QRIS (a national QR-payment scheme) is now accepted at most cafés and chain restaurants and works with e-wallets like GoPay, OVO, DANA; some foreign banking apps also generate QRIS. Credit cards are accepted at upscale places but often add a 2–3% surcharge.

A local SIM (Telkomsel has the strongest rural coverage, XL/Axis are cheaper in cities) or an eSIM (Airalo, Nomad, Saily) gives you data almost immediately. Local physical SIMs require passport registration under Indonesian law — buy from an official Telkomsel/XL kiosk rather than a random airport stall to avoid scams.

Dress modestly at temples (shoulders and knees covered, sarong provided at Balinese temples). Use the right hand for eating, giving, and receiving. Remove shoes before entering homes and many small shops. Public displays of affection are frowned upon outside tourist areas. Tipping isn't required but 10% is appreciated at restaurants that don't add a service charge.

Jakarta is Indonesia's capital and largest city — a business hub rather than a classic tourist destination. Highlights: Kota Tua (old Dutch quarter with cafés and museums), Monas (National Monument), Istiqlal Mosque (South-East Asia's largest, next door to the Catholic cathedral), Taman Mini Indonesia Indah (culture park), night markets in Glodok (Chinatown), and Pantai Indah Kapuk for modern food streets. Traffic is heavy — plan indoor blocks and use Gojek/Grab or MRT/TransJakarta buses.

Bandung sits on the cool West-Java highlands (~750 m). Popular for factory outlet shopping on Jalan Riau/Dago, cafés with mountain views, Kawah Putih (white crater lake south of the city), Tangkuban Perahu volcano, tea plantations at Ciwidey, and Sundanese food (nasi timbel, sate maranggi). Weekend traffic from Jakarta gets bad — travel midweek if you can.

Surabaya (East Java) is Indonesia's second-largest city and the main gateway to Mount Bromo and Ijen. Highlights: House of Sampoerna (kretek museum), Arab quarter around Ampel Mosque, colonial buildings on Jalan Tunjungan, and rawon (dark beef soup). Most tourists overnight one night before heading east to the volcanoes.

Malang (East Java) is a cool-climate university city and the more traveller-friendly base for Mount Bromo. Draws: Batu (mountain resort town, apple farms), Jodipan colour village, Coban Rondo waterfall, night markets, and bakso Malang (meatball soup with additions). Fly into Malang (MLG) directly or from Surabaya.

Mount Bromo (Tengger caldera, East Java) is Indonesia's most-photographed sunrise volcano. The classic trip: leave Cemoro Lawang around 03:00, jeep to King Kong Hill for sunrise over the caldera, then drive down onto the Sea of Sand and hike up Bromo's rim. Add Ijen (blue-fire crater sulphur mines) on a 2–3 day loop from Malang or Banyuwangi. Warm layers essential — it drops to 5–10 °C before dawn.

Kawah Ijen (Ijen Crater, East Java) is famous for its blue-flame sulphur combustion (visible only at night) and turquoise acid lake. The hike leaves around 01:00, takes 2 hours up plus 45 minutes down into the crater with a gas mask. Rangers may close the crater floor when sulphur levels are high — always check locally. Combine with Bromo as a 3-day tour from Malang or Banyuwangi.

The Gili Islands (Trawangan, Meno, Air) sit off Lombok's north-west coast. No motor vehicles — you get around on foot, bicycle, or cidomo (horse cart). Trawangan is the party-and-snorkel island; Air is the quietest with the best sunsets; Meno is the smallest and best for a couple's slow day. Fast boats leave from Padang Bai and Serangan in Bali (~1.5–2 hours) and Bangsal in Lombok. Great snorkelling with turtles right off the beach.

Raja Ampat (West Papua) is arguably the world's richest reef ecosystem — 75% of known coral species live here. Access via Sorong (SOQ) then a public ferry or resort transfer to Waisai. Trips are typically 5–10 nights on a liveaboard or at a homestay on Kri, Gam, Waigeo, or Misool. Non-negotiable: pay the marine park entry (currently around 1M IDR foreigner, valid one year) and follow reef-safe rules. Not a budget trip; not a first-time-Indonesia trip either.

Gudeg is Yogyakarta's signature dish — young jackfruit stewed for hours with coconut milk, palm sugar and spices until sweet, dark and tender. Served with rice, krecek (spicy cattle-skin stew), chicken and egg. Try it at Gudeg Yu Djum (multiple branches) or the row of night stalls on Jalan Wijilan near the Kraton. Sweet-heavy — expect a heavier palate than most other Indonesian dishes.

Bakso is Indonesian meatball soup — springy beef (sometimes chicken) meatballs in clear broth with noodles, tofu, fried shallots, and sambal. Sold everywhere from street pushcarts to sit-down warungs. Bakso Malang is a famous regional style with siomay (dumplings) and tahu (tofu) additions. Very safe street food — the broth is hot enough to be safe from most bugs.

Soto is Indonesian aromatic soup — many regional variants: soto ayam (chicken, turmeric broth, usually with rice or lontong), soto betawi (Jakarta, coconut-milk beef), soto lamongan (East Java, koya crumb topping), coto Makassar (dark beef offal soup). Almost always served with sambal, lime, and fried shallots. A breakfast/lunch staple.

Pempek is Palembang's (South Sumatra) chewy fish cake — Spanish mackerel or tenggiri blended with sago flour, boiled or fried, served with cuka: a dark sweet-sour-spicy dipping sauce with palm sugar, vinegar, chilli and garlic. Common varieties: pempek kapal selam (large, with an egg inside), lenjer (long log), adaan (small round fried).

Ayam geprek is Indonesia's fried-chicken-and-sambal dish — crispy chicken smashed (geprek) into fresh sambal on the plate. Popularised nationally in the 2010s. Menus usually list a spice level (level 1 mild, level 5+ eye-watering) and add rice, cucumber, and lalapan (raw leaves). Great cheap dinner at 20–30k IDR.

Vegetarian/vegan options are easy in tourist areas (Ubud, Canggu, Yogyakarta) — dedicated menus, tempeh, tofu, gado-gado, sayur lodeh, and mie/nasi goreng that can be made without egg or meat. Say 'tanpa daging' (no meat) and 'tanpa telur' (no egg) if needed. Watch for hidden shrimp paste (terasi) in sambal, and small pieces of prawn/anchovy in nasi goreng — ask 'ada terasi?' if strictly plant-based.

Coastal areas are excellent for seafood. Well-known spots: Jimbaran Bay (Bali, sunset grilled-fish rows on the sand), Muara Karang (Jakarta wholesale + restaurants), Kenjeran (Surabaya), and every fishing-village warung on Flores and Lombok. Grilled (bakar), fried (goreng), or in a spicy sour broth (asam pedas) are the classic preparations. Verify the price per kg BEFORE the fish is cooked at the more tourist-facing spots.

Family-friendly stays in Bali: Sanur (calm reef-protected beach), Nusa Dua (resort strip with pools and shallow water), Ubud (rice-terrace walks, monkey forest — supervise kids). Beyond Bali: Yogyakarta (Borobudur + Malioboro batik workshops), Malang (Batu apple farms + Museum Angkut), Bogor (rain-forest Botanic Gardens). Skip Kuta Bali with young kids (nightlife-heavy) and Nusa Penida with toddlers (winding cliff roads).

Romantic couples' options: Ubud (jungle villas with pools), Nusa Lembongan (quiet island cliff resorts), Uluwatu (dramatic clifftop suites), Amankila / Munduk / Sidemen (quieter east + north Bali), Nihi Sumba (award-winning remote resort). Away from Bali: Amanwana on Moyo Island, and Bawah Reserve in the Anambas. All above are expensive; budget alternatives are Sanur boutique guesthouses or Sidemen homestays with rice-field views.

Classic backpacker circuit: Bali (Canggu/Kuta), Gili Trawangan, Lombok (Kuta beaches), Flores (Labuan Bajo + Komodo tour), Yogyakarta (Borobudur/Prambanan), sometimes Bromo/Ijen loop. Fast-boats and budget flights (AirAsia, Lion, Citilink) link most. Cheap food at warungs (~25k IDR), hostel dorms from 100k IDR/night. Book Komodo trips locally (walk-in prices are lower than online). Cash needed in Flores and rural Lombok.

For a quieter Indonesia experience: Sidemen and Munduk in Bali (rice terraces and waterfalls, few tourists), Amed (Bali north-east, snorkelling), Nusa Lembongan out of season, Sumba (rugged and traditional villages), Moluku spice islands, and homestay-only areas of Flores away from Labuan Bajo. Avoid: Kuta Bali, Legian, and Canggu at peak season if you want quiet.

Common tourist scams to be aware of: (1) Airport taxis quoting flat fares 3–5× the meter — book Grab/Gojek or use official Blue Bird stands. (2) Money-changer sleight-of-hand at unlicensed booths — use PT Central Kuta or bank-branded exchanges only. (3) Motorbike-rental damage claims for pre-existing scratches — photograph the bike before you ride away. (4) 'Closed for ceremony, come to my shop' auto-detour in Ubud. (5) Fake police asking for on-the-spot fines — request to go to the station together (they'll usually leave).

Indonesia's unified emergency number is 112 (works from mobiles, no signal needed for local coverage). Specific: 110 police, 113 fire, 118/119 ambulance. Tourist assistance in Bali: 0361-224111. Save your embassy's number before travelling. Serious medical: SOS International or BIMC (Kuta/Nusa Dua/Ubud) — expensive private hospitals with English-speaking staff. Government hospitals (RSU/RS) are cheaper but variable.

Visa rules change — verify with the official Directorate General of Immigration before travel. As of 2026 mid-year, many nationalities can use Visa on Arrival (VoA, ~500k IDR, 30 days extendable once) or the e-VoA (apply online at molina.imigrasi.go.id). Longer stays use a B211A visitor visa (60 days, sponsor required, extendable). Overstay is charged per day and can result in deportation. Passport must have 6 months validity.

Indonesia has 38 provinces (as of 2022–2023, following the split of Papua into six). The largest islands and their provinces: Java (6 provinces incl. West/Central/East Java, DKI Jakarta, DIY Yogyakarta, Banten), Sumatra (10), Kalimantan (5), Sulawesi (6), Nusa Tenggara (Bali, NTB Lombok/Sumbawa, NTT Flores/Sumba/Timor), Maluku (2), Papua (6).

Borobudur is the world's largest Buddhist temple (9th century, UNESCO). Since 2022, climbing the upper terraces requires a timed, guided ticket (foreigner ~US$25–35) — buy online at wonderfulborobudur.com or through your accommodation. Sunrise access is limited and separately priced. Base of the temple stays open for a lower fee. Combine with Prambanan (Hindu, sunset Ramayana ballet in dry season) as a full day.
